content: The development of evidence-based national infection prevention and control (IPC) guidelines and their associated implementation strategies is a fundamental responsibility of the national IPC program. This includes ensuring the availability of the necessary infrastructure and supplies to facilitate the implementation of these guidelines, which should complement existing recommendations on antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and healthcare worker protection. The national IPC program must also prioritize the education and training of healthcare workers, focusing on the recommendations outlined in the guidelines. Early engagement and active participation of stakeholders in the development and production of these guidelines are critical to achieving consensus and ensuring successful implementation. Monitoring adherence to guideline implementation is essential to evaluate their adoption and effectiveness in achieving desired outcomes. This process also helps identify areas for improvement and necessary adjustments to implementation strategies. Healthcare worker protection should be addressed through specific guidelines or protocols, ideally under the responsibility of occupational health professionals in collaboration with the IPC team. This protection should include pre-employment screening, regular health assessments during employment, and appropriate vaccinations to mitigate infectious risks. Regular updates to IPC guidelines are necessary to ensure they reflect the most current evidence. The field of IPC has accumulated substantial knowledge on effective preventive interventions, many of which are simple and cost-effective. However, the existence of guidelines alone is insufficient to guarantee their adoption. Implementation science emphasizes the importance of local adaptation for successful guideline adoption. A recent WHO survey revealed that, on average, 74% of national IPC documents address the development, dissemination, and implementation of technical guidelines, while 43% highlight the importance of local adaptation. Over 80% of these documents emphasize the need for training all staff in IPC measures. The evidence review conducted for these guidelines evaluated the effectiveness of IPC programs, particularly the use of guidelines in combination with healthcare worker education and training. The primary outcomes assessed were the impact on healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) and hand hygiene compliance. Studies demonstrated that while healthcare workers were aware of updated national guidelines, implementation was inconsistent, with less than half of surveyed hospitals adopting the recommendations. Research also highlighted low adherence to maximal sterile barrier precautions during central venous catheter insertions, even among those aware of the guidelines. This underscores that knowledge of guidelines alone is insufficient to drive behavioral change. Attitudes toward guidelines were more positive among nurses than doctors and in pediatric ICUs compared to adult ICUs. The introduction of new guidelines as part of multimodal intervention strategies in settings without prior exposure to standardized protocols improved hand hygiene and reduced catheter-associated urinary tract infections. However, the overall quality of evidence supporting these findings was considered very low due to limitations in study design. The GDG (Guideline Development Group) emphasized the importance of embedding IPC education and training within clinical practice rather than delivering it in isolation. Training should be tailored to the specific tasks of healthcare workers and should include participatory, team-based strategies such as bedside and simulation training. This approach has been associated with reduced HAIs and improved hand hygiene compliance. The GDG identified three categories of healthcare workers requiring IPC training: IPC specialists, all healthcare workers involved in patient care, and other personnel supporting health service delivery. IPC specialists should receive expert-level training and regular updates to maintain their competencies. All healthcare workers should understand IPC measures embedded within clinical procedures, while support staff should be trained on the importance of IPC practices to ensure safety and quality in healthcare delivery. The GDG strongly recommended incorporating in-service mentorship programs, such as IPC link practitioners, to achieve behavioral change. Periodic evaluations of training effectiveness and staff knowledge should be conducted routinely to ensure optimal education delivery and practice. The GDG concluded that evidence-based practice guidelines should be developed and implemented as part of a broader multimodal improvement approach to reduce HAIs and AMR. This should include healthcare worker education and training. The GDG also identified research gaps, particularly in evaluating the effectiveness of local adaptation and implementation of technical guidelines. They proposed conducting situational analyses of guidelines and their implementation mechanisms to achieve the desired culture change. The GDG emphasized that IPC education should be part of an overall health facility education strategy, including orientation for new employees and continuous educational opportunities for existing staff. Special circumstances, such as outbreaks or public health emergencies, may require ad hoc training. Embedding IPC training across service areas and procedures is considered more effective than isolated training sessions.
